title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
short: When only gravity and springs do work, K + U stays the same.
trouble: Students think a heavier object reaches the bottom of a frictionless ramp with a higher speed.

blocks.html: The work-energy theorem counts the work of every force. Gravity's work and a spring's work can be tracked instead as changes in gravitational and elastic potential energy. If nothing else does work, the total stays fixed.

When only gravity and springs do work, the mechanical energy is conserved: $\role[starting kinetic energy]{energy}{K_i} + \role[starting potential energy]{energy}{U_i} = \role[final kinetic energy]{energy}{K_f} + \role[final potential energy]{energy}{U_f}$, with $U = U_g + U_s$.

Gravity's work on the object is $-\Delta U_g$ and the spring's is $-\Delta U_s$. If they are the only forces doing work, the work-energy theorem gives $-\Delta U_g - \Delta U_s = \Delta K$, so $\Delta K + \Delta U = 0$. Normal forces on a frictionless track and the tension in a pendulum string are perpendicular to the motion, so they do no work and don't spoil this.

blocks.name: ph-energy

opts.task: Change the mass. The speed at every point stays the same, because both energies scale with m.

blocks.cap: A cart on a frictionless track: K and Ug trade back and forth, and their total stays fixed.

blocks.title: Down a slide
blocks.q: A child starts from rest at the top of a frictionless slide $5\ \text{m}$ high. Find the speed at the bottom.

blocks.title: From hill to hill
blocks.q: A coaster moves at $4\ \text{m/s}$ on a $30\ \text{m}$ hill. Ignoring friction, how fast is it on the next hill, $18\ \text{m}$ high?

blocks.title: A spring launcher
blocks.q: A spring with $k = 800\ \text{N/m}$ compressed $10\ \text{cm}$ launches a $0.2\ \text{kg}$ ball horizontally. Find its launch speed.

items: Choose the system and check that only gravity and springs do work on it.
Pick a zero height for $U_g$; any level works, but keep it for the whole problem.

Write $\role[starting kinetic energy]{energy}{K_i} + \role[starting potential energy]{energy}{U_i} = \role[final kinetic energy]{energy}{K_f} + \role[final potential energy]{energy}{U_f}$ and solve for the unknown.

blocks.html: Thinking a heavier object reaches the bottom of a frictionless ramp with a higher speed. It has more energy, but it needs more energy for each m/s: $mgh = \tfrac12 mv^2$, and the mass cancels. Check: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ has no $m$ in it.
Try it in the Science Lab's Trebuchet Workshop: a falling counterweight's potential energy becomes the projectile's kinetic energy.
